findings.summary: The chunking example caps the body text at 400 tokens and then prepends the title, so chunks can exceed the stated 400-token cap.
findings.evidence: "for part in cap_tokens(sec.text, 400):" ... "\"text\": sec.title + \"\\n\" + part" with the note "400-token cap per chunk"
findings.fix: Cap the body at 400 minus the title's token count, for example cap_tokens(sec.text, 400 - tokens(sec.title)). Alternatively, say that the cap applies to the body and the title is extra.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "reciprocal", "combines").
findings.evidence: Hybrid search combines dense vectors (meaning) with BM25 keywords (exact IDs, names, error codes). Merge the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank).
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: HyDE and query rewriting are named but never explained, so a learner cannot tell what either does or why it helps.
findings.evidence: "Query rewriting and HyDE help vague or multi-turn questions"
findings.fix: Add one line for each. Query rewriting: an LLM turns the question into a standalone search query. HyDE: the LLM writes a hypothetical answer, and that text is embedded for retrieval instead of the question.

findings.summary: Page 4 and page 6 give different retrieval depths for the same step.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "fetch top-k chunks (k often 5-20)" and the rerank diagram "Top 50"; page 6: "Retrieve top 20-50, rerank to 5"
findings.fix: Use one range everywhere. For example, on page 4 write "fetch top 20-50 candidates" for the reranker input, and keep "k = 5-20" only for the case with no reranker.

findings.summary: A single bullet holds two separate ideas, what dense search is for and what BM25 is for.
findings.evidence: "Dense = meaning; BM25 = IDs, names, error codes"
findings.fix: Split it into two bullets, one for dense and one for BM25. Or add a small two-row table of Dense vs BM25 with columns for strength and misses.

findings.summary: Two adjacent bullets give conflicting chunk ordering rules.
findings.evidence: "Dedupe near-identical chunks; order by relevance" followed by "Best chunks first and last; middle recalled worst"
findings.fix: Merge them into one rule: "Order by relevance, then place the best chunks at the start and end of the context". Split the dedupe step into its own bullet.

findings.summary: recall@k is used as the tuning criterion on page 2 but is not defined until page 5.
findings.evidence: "Tune on recall@k with your own queries" and "Choose size? Compare candidates by recall@k."
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss on page 2, e.g. "recall@k = share of relevant chunks found in the top k (defined in full on the measuring page)", or move the measurement chapter before chunking.

findings.summary: ANN is used in the pre-filter vs post-filter comparison but is never defined anywhere in the chapter.
findings.evidence: "Pre-filter | Inside the ANN search" and "Pre filters inside ANN; post can return fewer than k"
findings.fix: Add a short definition where pre-filtering is introduced, e.g. "ANN = approximate nearest neighbour search, the fast vector lookup over the index".

findings.summary: The letter k means two different things: the top-k result count and the RRF constant. The page never marks the difference, and the quiz page repeats it.
findings.evidence: "RRF score = sum of 1/(k+rank) over lists, k ≈ 60" next to "Post-filter ... Can return fewer than k"; page 7: "RRF with k=60" and "top 5 chunks"
findings.fix: Rename the RRF constant (for example c = 60) on pages 3, 6 and 7, or label it "RRF constant (not top-k)".

findings.summary: The recall@k score cell packs the definition, the averaging and the hit-rate equivalence into one dense table cell.
findings.evidence: relevant found in top k, averaged; one relevant chunk = hit rate
findings.fix: Keep the cell to the definition (share of relevant chunks found in top k, averaged over queries) and move the hit-rate note to its own bullet below the table.

findings.summary: The Planning Patterns chapter drops the outline's Interview Point, so its three questions are never answered.
findings.evidence: Page 2 ends with the "Cap the rounds" box ("Limit reflection to 1-3 rounds. Every round adds LLM calls and latency."). The outline's "Interview Point: When would you choose plan-and-execute over ReAct? How do you handle a plan that stops matching reality? What does reflection add, and what does it cost?" has no matching section. Pages 1, 3 and 4 each have one.
findings.fix: Add a "4. Interview Point" section to page 2 with short answers. Plan-and-execute for long, predictable tasks. Re-plan after each step or failure by checking the plan against observations. Reflection adds quality through draft, critique and revise, and costs extra LLM calls and latency.

findings.summary: The 'Use for' column holds 'Most common' for orchestrator-worker, which is a frequency note and not a use case, unlike the other two rows.
findings.evidence: Orchestrator-worker | Lead splits, delegates, merges | Most common
findings.fix: Replace 'Most common' with a use case such as 'Parallel, decomposable tasks' and state that it is the usual default in a separate bullet.

findings.summary: The Stopping Conditions chapter drops the outline's Interview Point, so termination, superlinear cost and latency are never asked as questions.
findings.evidence: Page 5 ends with the Latency table ("Parallel calls | run independent tools together" and so on). The outline's "Interview Point: How do you guarantee an agent terminates? Why does cost grow faster than linearly with steps? What would you do to cut latency without losing quality?" is absent from the page.
findings.fix: Add a "4. Interview Point" section to page 5. Guarantee termination with a hard step cap plus a budget limit and repeat detection. Cost is superlinear because each step re-sends the whole growing context. Cut latency with parallel tool calls, streaming, fewer steps and routing simple requests to a fast model.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet lists 'Orchestrator-worker by default' directly above 'Start with a single agent', so a skimming learner could read the default as multi-agent, which contradicts page 4.
findings.evidence: Orchestrator-worker by default / Start with a single agent
findings.fix: Reorder and reword: 'Start with a single agent' first, then 'If multi-agent is justified, default to orchestrator-worker'.

findings.summary: The table says the user never sees an indirect injection, but indirect payloads can be visible, for example text on a rendered page or in an email body.
findings.evidence: User sees it | Yes | Never; "Indirect vs direct? Hidden in fetched content; the user never sees it"
findings.fix: Change "Never" to "Usually not" or "Often hidden". Say indirect injection is defined by the source (third-party content), not by whether the user can see it.
